name: Bianca Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two CNC lathes at a machine shop that makes steel fittings for tractors and buses. A CNC lathe spins a bar of metal while a computer-guided tool cuts it to shape, so my job is loading bars, setting offsets, measuring parts and keeping the coolant and the swarf under control. Swarf is the curly metal waste, and it gets everywhere, in your boots, in your hair. We're about sixty people, on the old industrial road out past the football ground.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit in your day, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, actually, though not in the way people think. When a lathe throws an alarm code I'll ask a chatbot on my phone what it means before I go hunting for Gary, our setter. The manuals for the newer machine are in German and I get the app to translate them. I also write the union newsletter with it on Sunday nights, which my husband Imran thinks is hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I've always said it's a handy tool, not magic. It finds alarm codes, it translates, it doesn't cut steel. I'd probably post that in the shop group chat with a laughing face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a slight relief. But it doesn't fix what's actually wrong at our place, which is the pay. I've been here nine years and I'm still below what the shop across town pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and keep using the tools for the boring bits. I'd push the union to use AI for our side too, like going through the company accounts when it's pay talks time. I've already tried it with last year's figures and it found things the rep missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit disappointed, if I'm honest, I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the time it found something in the accounts.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I fed last year's published accounts into a chatbot and asked it where the profit went. It showed the owners paid themselves a big dividend the same year they told us there was no money for a raise. I took that to our rep, Anton, and we used it in the talks. We got two percent more than the first offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the household manage, with pay that low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Imran drives the number 14 bus, his pay's no better than mine. We'd just keep doing what we do, two low wages and a careful spreadsheet. The kids don't go without much, but we don't do holidays abroad.

S0.say: She's always said AI is a handy tool, not magic: it finds alarm codes and translates manuals but doesn't cut steel. She'd post that in the shop group chat with a laughing face.
S0.think: It would be a slight relief, but it doesn't fix the real problem at her shop, which is low pay after nine years. She's still paid below the shop across town.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI for the boring parts of the job. Pushes the union to use AI to go through the company accounts at pay-talk time, as she already did last year.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little disappointed because she likes new tools.
S0.quote: It showed the owners paid themselves a big dividend the same year they told us there was no money for a raise.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is an unusual mix: a daily AI user who sees it mainly as a weapon for workers in pay talks. Her grievance is low pay, not technology. She told a concrete story of using AI on company accounts to win a better offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, as long as workers get a share. If the machines get smarter, the people running them should get trained and paid more, not fewer of us for the same money. I'd write that in the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do all right. I'm the one people already come to for the new machine. The worry is less me and more the older guys who won't touch a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the manager and ask to be trained on whatever new system comes in, first. I'd start an evening course in CNC programming, there's one at the technical college for about four hundred, and I'd ask the union to get the company to pay half. And I'd set up a little lunchtime thing showing people the AI apps on their phones, because the more of us who can do it, the harder we are to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly about money. Excited too, I can't pretend I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Four hundred for a course. Is that money you have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, four hundred is a lot for us. It's most of what's in the account. That's why I'd fight for the company to pay half, and if they wouldn't, I'd pay it in three bits and we'd skip the summer camp for Sami.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, the setter. He's fifty-eight and brilliant with his hands, he can hear a tool going blunt. But he won't touch the screen. I'd hate to see him pushed out by a machine I helped bring in.

S1.say: Good, as long as workers get a share: people running smarter machines should get trained and paid more, not fewer people doing the same for the same money. She'd write that in the union newsletter.
S1.think: She expects to do all right, since people already come to her about the new machine. Her worry is more for the older workers who won't touch a tablet.
S1.do: Asks the manager to be trained first on any new system and starts a CNC programming course at the technical college for about four hundred, pressing the union to get the company to pay half. Runs lunchtime sessions showing colleagues AI apps on their phones.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy about money and openly excited too.
S1.quote: The more of us who can do it, the harder we are to replace.
S1.fieldNote: Bianca reaches for opportunity first, but the four-hundred course fee shows how thin her margin is. She wants to spread skills so the whole floor gets stronger. She worries about the setter Gary, and feels guilty about helping bring in machines that could push him out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a law, now: if a company replaces workers with AGI, it pays into a fund that keeps those workers' wages going. I'd say it loud, in the newsletter and online, and I'd help organise. I'm not anti-technology, I'm anti-dumping people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the thing I thought made me safe, being good with the new stuff, stops mattering. If the machine can program itself and a robot can load it, they don't need a clever operator, they don't need any operator. Two years isn't enough to turn into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get the shop floor organised, everyone in the union, and push for a deal before the robots arrive: notice, pay-outs, retraining money. At home we'd cut to the bone, no more phone upgrades, no school trips abroad, and we'd look at renting out Aisha's room to a student if she shared with Sami. I'd also start doing CAD drawings for people on the side, small jobs for hobby makers, while that still pays something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I've been running fast in the right direction and the road just ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd do CAD drawings on the side. Would that even last, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for a year, maybe less. But a year of extra money is a year. I'd rather have something coming in while we fight than sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you awake at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that really keeps me up. Not my job, Aisha's future. She wants to be a vet. What do I tell her, study six years for something that might not exist?

S2.say: There needs to be a law now: companies that replace workers with AGI pay into a fund to keep those workers' wages going. She'd say it in the newsletter and online, and help organise.
S2.think: Being good with new technology stops mattering when the machine can program itself and a robot can load it. Two years isn't enough to become something else.
S2.do: Organises the whole shop into the union to win notice, pay-outs and retraining money before robots arrive. Cuts spending to the bone, considers renting out a room, and takes small CAD drawing jobs on the side while they still pay.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like running fast in the right direction and the road just ending.
S2.quote: I've been running fast in the right direction and the road just ended.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture takes away the edge Bianca relies on, and she sees it immediately. She still acts on every front at once: organising, cutting costs and earning on the side. Her deepest worry is her daughter's plan to become a vet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build something fair, so let's not waste it arguing about whether it's real. I'd want the union and the council working on a plan for this town now. That would be the main story in my newsletter for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a few more steps. I could get into programming and robot setup, be one of the last people on the floor. Still ends the same, but it buys time for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the programming course and try to get the company to put me on the robot cell when it comes. I'd save every bit of overtime into a separate account, even if it's only a few hundred by the end of the year. And I'd push the union nationally, not just our branch, for a law on notice and pay-outs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I feel better when I've got a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be the one setting up the robots that replace your colleagues. Is that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know it. If I'm the one setting up the robot cell, I'm the one teaching it to replace Gary and the others. I'd tell them straight. And I'd want the deal agreed before I lift a finger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything for Aisha?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. With five years she'd be finishing school as it arrived. I'd talk to her about it honestly, and say pick something you love, and we'll fight for a world where that's allowed.

S3.say: Five years is enough to build something fair, so nobody should waste it arguing about whether it's real. The union and the council should start a plan for the town now.
S3.think: Five years lets her move into programming and robot setup and be one of the last on the floor. It still ends the same, but it buys time for her children.
S3.do: Starts the programming course and asks to be put on the robot cell when it arrives. Saves every bit of overtime in a separate account and pushes the national union for a law on notice and pay-outs.
S3.feel: Busy-anxious, and better when she has a list.
S3.quote: If I'm the one setting up the robot cell, I'm the one teaching it to replace Gary and the others.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Bianca map out a sequence of steps, and that steadies her. She faces the contradiction of training the robots that replace her colleagues directly and wants a deal agreed first. She would be honest with her daughter rather than steer her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get the money side right: a share of what the machines earn going to everyone. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen and I'd want our union pushing it in every election. That's the fight of my life, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'd be fifty-three, and I'd have spent ten years keeping half a step ahead. I'd probably manage a job in the robot side until near the end. But I don't trust the owners to share, and I've seen the dividend numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the programming course properly, then maybe the two-year technical diploma at night, and move into maintenance or setup somewhere bigger, even if that's an hour's drive. I'd get involved in the party locally, not just the union. And we'd tell the kids to study what they love but to keep their options wide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but with energy behind it. I know what I'm fighting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you feel safe, given how quickly you pick things up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. The machine gets there anyway. What the ten years buys is the chance to make sure people like me aren't left with nothing when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd drive an hour each way for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An hour each way, yes. Imran says I'm mad. But if that's where the work is for the last few years, I'll do the drive. We'd sort the kids around it, Aisha would be old enough to help with Sami.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to get the money side right, with a share of what machines earn going to everyone. She'd want her union pushing it in every election and calls it the fight of her life.
S4.think: At 53 she'd likely have kept half a step ahead and held a robot-side job until near the end. But she doesn't trust owners to share, having seen the dividend numbers.
S4.do: Completes the programming course and then a two-year technical diploma at night, moving into maintenance or setup at a bigger plant even an hour's drive away. Gets involved in her local party as well as the union.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but with energy behind it because she knows what she's fighting for.
S4.quote: I don't trust the owners to share, and I've seen the dividend numbers.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Bianca imagine a full career move, but her anxiety stays because her doubt is about who gets the gains, not her own skills. She plans to take a longer commute and move into party politics. Her energy is directed outward.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away the one thing I'm good at, which is learning fast. What would help is a law that makes companies keep paying people when machines take their jobs, and a union strong enough to enforce it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who use AI every day what they think of it. Everybody assumes we're cheerleaders. I use it every day and I think it should be working for us, not for the owners.

headlineQuote: I use it every day and I think it should be working for us, not for the owners.
portrait: Bianca Khan is a 43-year-old CNC lathe operator at a sixty-person machine shop making tractor and bus fittings, married to Imran, a bus driver, with two children and very little savings. She uses AI every day, for alarm codes, German manuals, her union newsletter and even reading company accounts for pay talks. She is calm about a plateau and only uneasy about steady change, which she sees as her chance to move up. Fast AGI alarms her because it wipes out her edge as a quick learner, and with more time she plans courses, a longer commute and a bigger role in politics. Her anxiety comes less from her own skills than from doubt that owners will share the gains.
biggestWorry: The two-year picture, because it removes her main advantage of learning faster than others.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies keep paying workers they replace with machines, and a union strong enough to enforce it.
